opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's made me much calmer about it. Early on, during my PhD, a rejection felt like a personal verdict, like the reviewers were saying the idea was worthless and so was I. You'd get those three reviews back, one of them clearly hadn't read the paper carefully, and you'd spend days being angry or depressed about it.

But after it happens enough times, you start to see the pattern. Some of the work I'm proudest of got rejected at least once. And some papers that sailed through, nobody remembers now. So you realize the review process is noisy. It's a few busy people, often reviewing under time pressure, judging something that's very new. If the idea is genuinely different from what people expect, there's a good chance it gets pushback at first. In a way, a little resistance can even be a signal that you're not just doing the incremental thing everyone else is doing.

That doesn't mean I ignore the reviews. I've learned to separate the emotion from the content. I'll read them, feel annoyed for maybe an evening, and then go back the next day and ask: what did they misunderstand, and why? Usually, if a smart reviewer misread the paper, it's partly my fault. The writing wasn't clear, the experiment that would convince a skeptic wasn't there, or I was too attached to my own framing. A lot of papers got much better because they were rejected.

I also try to tell my students this, because for them it hurts the most. Your value as a researcher isn't decided by one conference decision. What matters over the long run is whether the work holds up, whether people actually build on it years later. If you keep that time horizon in mind, a rejection becomes just one step in the process rather than the end of the story.

r001.rationale: He says repeated rejections made him calmer and better able to separate emotion from useful feedback, showing rejection strengthened how he handles future rejection.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think rejection has shaped me more than acceptance has. When I was a PhD student, almost every paper I wrote got rejected the first time. ResNeXt, for example, was rejected before it got into CVPR. Some of my work on self-supervised learning went through multiple rounds. And early on, every rejection felt personal. You read the reviews, and you're angry for a day or two. You think the reviewers didn't understand, or they were lazy, or they had some agenda.

But after it happens enough times, something shifts. You start to realize that the review process is incredibly noisy. The same paper, with the same ideas, can get a strong accept one cycle and a reject the next. Once you internalize that, a rejection stops being a judgment on whether the work is good. It becomes a data point, and a fairly weak one.

What I try to do now, and what I tell my students, is separate two things. One is the signal in the reviews. Even the harshest, most unfair review usually has one sentence that's actually right, something that was unclear or an experiment that was missing. You extract that and you fix it. The other is the noise, the parts where the reviewer just didn't engage, or wanted a different paper. You let that go. You don't rewrite your paper to satisfy someone who was never going to be convinced.

The deeper lesson, I think, is that you have to have your own internal compass about what matters. If you only work on things that reviewers will immediately like, you end up doing incremental work, because reviewers are most comfortable with things that look like what already exists. Some of the ideas I'm most proud of were the ones that got the most pushback initially. So now, when I get a rejection on something I really believe in, I take it almost as a sign that the idea is unfamiliar enough to be worth pursuing. Not always, of course. Sometimes the idea is just wrong. But you have to be willing to sit with that uncertainty.

And then on a personal level, I think it just made me more resilient and, frankly, more empathetic as a reviewer and as an advisor. When my students get rejected, I don't say "the reviewers are stupid." I say, "okay, this hurts, let's take two days, and then let's read the reviews together and figure out what's real." Because the rejection itself is not the thing that defines you. How you respond to it, and whether you keep going, is what actually matters over a career.

r001.rationale: He says repeated rejection made him more resilient and explains how it taught him to separate useful feedback from noise and respond constructively, showing that rejection strengthened his ability to handle future rejections.

astra-6.text:
Repeated rejections have made me less afraid of rejection, but I wouldn’t say they’ve made me indifferent. It still hurts when you’ve put a lot of effort into something and people don’t see the value in it.

What changes is how you interpret that response. You learn to separate the decision from the feedback. A rejection doesn’t necessarily mean the idea is bad, but it also doesn’t mean the reviewers are wrong. Maybe there’s a real weakness, or maybe you haven’t communicated the idea clearly enough. The useful question becomes: what can I learn from this, and do I still believe in the work?

So I try to give myself a little time to feel disappointed, then come back and read the comments more calmly. You need enough confidence to keep going, and enough openness to change your mind.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated rejections have made him less afraid of rejection, clearly indicating they strengthened his ability to handle future rejections.

sol-6.1.text:
After enough rejections, you learn not to take each one as a judgment of you as a researcher. It can still be disappointing—you put a lot of time into something, and you want people to understand it. But I try to separate that feeling from the useful question: Is there something in the feedback that can make the work better?

Sometimes the reviewers identify a real weakness. Sometimes we haven’t explained the idea clearly enough. And sometimes you disagree with the decision. The important thing is to stay open to criticism without letting the decision completely determine your confidence in the work. Rejection becomes part of the process, rather than the end of it.

r001.rationale: The response says that after repeated rejections, he learns not to take them as personal judgments and treats rejection as part of the process, showing that experience makes him better able to handle future rejection.
